(Amended by Ordinances 175158, 189396, and 191973, effective January 1, 2025.)  

  1. The Council finds that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, source of income, and non-religion exists in Portland and that state law does not clearly prohibit such discrimination.  It is the intent of the Council, in the exercise of its powers for the protection of the public health, safety, and general welfare and for the maintenance of peace and good government, that every individual must have an equal opportunity to participate fully in the life of the City and that discriminatory barriers to equal participation in employment, housing, and public accommodations be removed.

(Amended by Ordinances 175158, 189396, 191973, and 192153, effective April 10, 2026.)

  1. A.  Sexual orientation means an individual's actual or perceived romantic, physical or sexual attraction to other persons, or lack thereof, on the basis of gender. 
  2. B.  Source of income is the means by which a person supports themselves and their dependents, including but not limited to money and property from any occupation, profession or activity, from any contract, settlement or agreement, from federal or state payments, court-ordered payments, gifts, bequests, annuities, life insurance policies, and compensation for illness or injury, but excluding any money or property derived in a manner made illegal or criminal by any law, statute or ordinance.
  3. C.  Gender identity means a person's actual or perceived sex, including a person's identity, appearance, expression or behavior, whether or not that identity, appearance, expression or behavior is different from that traditionally associated with the person's sex at birth.
  4. D.  Family or relationship structure means the actual or perceived involvement, or lack thereof, of consenting individuals in intimate personal relationships.Intimate personal relationships include, but are not limited to, multi-partner or multi-parent families and relationships, step-families, multi-generational households, diverse family structures, consensually nonmonogamous relationships, and consensual sexual and/or intimate relationships, including asexual and aromantic relationships.
  5. E. Commissioner means the Commissioner of the State of Oregon's Bureau of Labor and Industries.
  6. F.  In addition to any other definition provided by law, the term religion used herein expressly includes nonreligion, such as atheism, agnosticism, and nonbelief in God or gods as has been recognized by the courts.
  7. All other terms used in this Chapter are to be defined as in Oregon Revised Statutes Chapter 659 and 659A.

(Amended by Ordinances 175158, 189396, and 191973, effective January 1, 2025.)

  1. A.  The prohibitions in this Chapter against discriminating on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity do not apply:
    1. 1.  To the leasing or renting of a room or rooms within an individual living unit that is occupied by the lessor as their residence;
    2. 2.  To dwellings with not more than two individual living units where one of the units is owner occupied; 
    3. 3.  To space within a church, temple, synagogue, religious school, or other facility used primarily for religious purposes.
  2. B.  The prohibitions in this Chapter against discriminating on the basis of source of income do not prohibit:
    1. 1.  Inquiry into and verification of a source or amount of income;
    2. 2.  Inquiry into, evaluation of, and decisions based on the amount, stability, security or creditworthiness of any source of income;
    3. 3.  Screening prospective purchasers and tenants on bases not specifically prohibited by this chapter or state or federal law;
    4. 4.  Refusal to contract with a governmental agency under 42 U.S.C. §1437f(a) “Section 8.”
  3. C.  The prohibitions in this Chapter against discriminating on the basis of gender identity do not prohibit:
    1. 1.  Health or athletic clubs or other entities that operate gender-specific facilities involving public nudity such as showers and locker rooms, from requiring an individual to document their gender or transitional status. Such documentation can include but is not limited to a court order, letter from a physician, birth certificate, passport, or driver’s license.
    2. 2.  Otherwise valid employer dress codes or policies, so long as the employer provides, on a case-by-case basis, for reasonable accommodation based on the health and safety needs of persons protected on the basis of gender identity.
    3. 3.  The above exceptions do not   excuse a failure to provide reasonable and appropriate accommodations permitting all persons access to restrooms consistent with their expressed gender.
  4. D.  The exceptions in ORS 659A.006(4) and ORS 659A.030(1) apply to non-religion as well as religion.

(Amended by Ordinances 175158, 189396, 191973, and 192153, effective April 10, 2026.)

  1. A.  It is unlawful to discriminate in employment on the basis of an individual's race, religion, color, sex, national origin, marital status, age if the individual is 18 years of age or older, or disability, by committing any of the acts made unlawful under the provisions of ORS 659A.030 and 659A.142.
  2. B.  In addition, it is unlawful to discriminate in employment on the basis of an individual's sexual orientation, gender identity, source of income, familial status, or family or relationship structure, by committing against any such individual any of the acts already made unlawful under ORS 659A.030 when committed against the categories of persons listed therein.
  3. C. Nothing in this Section will be construed to limit the ability of an employer offering health insurance coverage in connection with a group health plan to limit plan enrollment and benefits coverage to an employee, their spouse or domestic partner, and their dependent children. 
  4. D. Nothing in this Section will be construed to limit the ability of an employer to establish and enforce otherwise valid policies prohibiting conflicts-of-interest in the workplace.

(Added by Ordinance 192144, effective March 13, 2026.)

  1. A. Definitions. 
    1. 1. Place of public accommodation has the same meaning as defined in ORS 659A.400.  
    2. 2. Appropriate signage means signage that indicates that single-occupant restrooms are not restricted to a single gender. Examples include, but are not limited to, signs with the words "bathroom," "restroom," "all-user restroom," "all-gender restroom," "gender-neutral restroom," "unisex," or that use images to indicate that restrooms are accessible to all users.   
    3. 3. Single-occupant restroom means a fully enclosed, lockable restroom with one toilet, designed for use by one individual at a time. A single-occupant restroom may be used by an individual with the assistance of or in the company of another individual (for example, a personal attendant, parent or child). A single-occupant restroom may include a urinal in addition to a toilet.  
  2. B. Single-occupant restrooms in places of public accommodation may not be restricted to a specific sex or gender identity and must use appropriate signage to indicate such facilities are designated for use by any person, regardless of sex or gender identity.  
  3. C. Entities covered by this Chapter 23.01 must comply on or before January 1, 2027, by replacing existing signs on the exterior of single-occupant restrooms restricting use to a single gender with signs indicating that they are for use by all users. Enforcement will commence on July 1, 2027.   
  4. D. Notwithstanding Section 23.01.080, this Section does not create a private right of action, and no private action arising from this Section shall be maintained.

(Added by Ordinances 187454 and 191973, effective January 1, 2025.)

  1. A. Definitions. As used in this Section 23.01.075, the following words and phrases must be construed as defined in this Subsection:
    1. 1.  Closed captioning means a transcript or dialog of the audio portion of a television program that is displayed on the bottom portion of a television receiver screen when the user activates the feature.
    2. 2.  Closed captioned television receiver means a receiver of television programming that has the ability to display closed captioning, including but not limited to a television, digital set top box, and other technology capable of displaying closed captioning for television programming.
    3. 3.  Public area means any part of a public facility that is open to the general public.
    4. 4.  Public facility has the same meaning as “place of public accommodation,” which is defined in ORS 659A.400 (2013).
    5. 5.  Regular hours means the hours of any day in which a public facility is generally open to members of the general public.
  2. B.  Any person owning or managing a public facility must activate closed captioning on any closed-captioned television receiver in use in any public area during regular hours.
  3. C.  A person owning or managing a public facility is not required to make a closed-captioned television receiver available for viewing in a public area if:
    1. 1.  No receiver of television programming of any kind is available in a public area of the public facility; or,
    2. 2.  The only receiver of television programming available in a public area of the public facility is incapable of displaying close captioning.
  4. D.  Civil penalties.  A violation of this Section may result in the assessment of civil penalties, as provided below:
    1. 1.  If the City Administrator reasonably believes a violation has occurred, the City Administrator may issue a written determination addressing the following:
      1. a.  A reference to this Section, describing the violations that have occurred or are occurring;
      2. b.  The date and the time of the occurrence, and the street address or location of the public facility;
      3. c.  A concise statement of the matters asserted or charged; and,
      4. d.  A request that the addressee provide a written response to the City Administrator within 10 business days either disputing the occurrence of the violation or describing how the violation has been abated and how such violations will be prevented from reoccurring.
    2. The determination may be personally delivered to the person, or may be served by Registered or Certified Mail.  For purposes of this Subsection, service by registered or certified mail is complete and effective when a correctly addressed notice is deposited with the postal service after being either certified or registered by the postal service.
    3. 2.  If the person fails to provide a written response, or the written response fails to reasonably satisfy the City Administrator regarding the identified violations, the City Administrator may file a complaint with the Code Hearings Officer, as provided under Portland City Code Section 22.03.020, for violations of this Section 23.01.075, asking the Code Hearings Officer to impose civil penalties not to exceed $500 for each day such violation is committed or permitted to continue as provided in this Section.  Having made a determination to ask that the Code Hearings Officer to impose civil penalties as provided by this Section, the City Administrator will give the person written notice of the determination by causing notice to be served upon the person at their business or residence address.  Service of the notice will be accomplished by mailing the notice by regular mail or, at the option of the City Administrator, by personal service in the same manner as a summons served in an action at law.  Mailing of the notice by regular mail will be prima facie evidence of receipt of the notice.  Service of notice upon the person apparently in charge of a business during its hours of operation will constitute prima facie evidence of notice to the business owner.
    4. 3.  In determining the amount of the civil penalty to be imposed for violations of the provisions of this Chapter, the Code Hearings Officer will consider:
      1. a.  The extent and nature of the person’s involvement in the violation;
      2. b.  The harms, whether economic, financial or otherwise, that occurred or were suffered as a result of the violation;
      3. c.  Whether the violations were isolated or temporary, or repeated or continuous;
      4. d.  The magnitude and seriousness of the violation;
      5. e.  The City’s costs of investigating the violations and correcting or attempting to correct the violation; and,  
      6. f.  Any other applicable facts bearing on the nature and seriousness of the violation.

(Amended by Ordinances 165319, 189396, and 191973, effective January 1, 2025.)

  1. A.  Enforcement of all or any part of this Chapter will be governed by the procedures established in ORS Chapter 659A.  Rules adopted by the City Administrator pursuant to Section 23.01.090 of this Chapter may also be used to implement enforcement and administration of this Chapter.
  2. B.  Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an unlawful employment practice under this Chapter may file a complaint with the Commissioner under procedures established in ORS 659A.820, and any person claiming to be aggrieved by an unlawful practice under this Chapter relating to selling, renting or leasing real estate or discrimination in public accommodations, may file a complaint with the Commissioner under procedures established in ORS 659A.820.
  3. C.  The Commissioner may then proceed and will have the same enforcement powers under this Chapter, and if the complaint is found to be justified the complainant will be entitled to the same remedies under ORS 659A.840 to 659A.860 as in the case of any other complaint filed under ORS 659A.820.
  4. D.  Any order issued by the Commissioner under this Chapter will be viewed as one issued by a hearings officer employed by the City within the meaning of ORS 3.136(3) and will be fully enforceable by the City.
  5. E.  Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an unlawful discriminatory act under the provisions of this code will have a cause of action in any court of competent jurisdiction for damages and such other remedies as may be appropriate.  Election of remedies and other procedural issues relating to the interplay between administrative proceedings and private rights of action will be handled as provided for in ORS 659A.870 and 659A.885.  The court may grant such relief as it deems appropriate, including, but not limited to, such relief as is provided in ORS 659A.885.

  1. A.  It is an unlawful practice for an employer to exclude an applicant from consideration solely because of the applicant’s criminal history.
  2. B.  An employer may consider an applicant’s criminal history in the hiring process only after making a conditional offer of employment.  An employer violates this Chapter if an employer accesses an applicant’s criminal history prior to making a conditional offer of employment.
  3. C.  It is not an unlawful practice for an employer to rescind a conditional offer of employment based upon an applicant’s criminal history if an employer determines in good faith that a specific offense or conduct is job related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity.
  4. D.  In making the determination of whether an applicant’s criminal history is job related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity, an employer must conduct an individualized assessment of:
    1. 1.  The nature and gravity of the criminal offense;  
    2. 2.  The time that has elapsed since the criminal offense took place; and
    3. 3.  The nature of the employment held or sought.
  5. E.  Nothing in this Section prevents an employer from considering an applicant’s criminal history after making a conditional offer of employment, except that an employer may not consider:
    1. 1.  An arrest not leading to a conviction, except where a crime is unresolved or charges are pending against an applicant;
    2. 2.  Convictions that have been judicially voided or expunged; or
    3. 3.  Charges that have been resolved through the completion of a diversion or deferral of judgment program for offenses not involving physical harm or attempted physical harm to a person.
  6. F.  If, after consideration of an applicant’s criminal history, an employer rescinds the conditional offer of employment, the employer must notify the applicant in writing of its decision and must identify the relevant criminal convictions on which the decision is based.

1. A. Consistent with state and federal law, the City prohibits the use of City resources to enforce federal immigration law.
    1. 1.City facilities, property, moneys, equipment, technology or personnel may not be used for the purpose of investigating, detecting, apprehending, arresting, detaining or holding persons for the purpose of enforcing federal immigration laws.
    2. 2. No City entity or law enforcement agency may enter into a formal or informal agreement with a federal immigration authority relating to the detention of a person for the purpose of enforcing federal immigration laws.
    3. 3. Exceptwhen required by state or federal law, no City entity or law enforcement agency may collect, inquire into, or disclose information concerning an individual's immigration or citizenship status, country of birth, or other personal information for the purpose of enforcing federal immigration laws.
    4. 4. The prohibitions and requirements set forth in this Chapter do not apply to the following:
      1. a. When required by court order, or a warrant authorized by a court;
      2. b. When disclosure is required by a judicial subpoena issued as part of a court proceeding or by another compulsory court-issued legal process;
      3. c. When disclosure is required to effect the international extradition to this state and return of a person charged with or convicted of crimes in this state and for whom a warrant of arrest has been issued;
      4. d. To the extent that the information is available to the general public and under the same terms and conditions as it is available to the general public;
      5. e. When the information is necessary to advance an investigation into a violation of state or local criminal law;
      6. f. When the information is submitted to a court of this state, whether orally or in writing, in connection with a proceeding in that court; or
      7. g. When the information is necessary to determine the individual's eligibility for a benefit the individual is seeking.
  2. B. All City staff are required to participate in ongoing training on the City's sanctuary policies. The content of this training will align with federal law, state law, and Portland City Code.
    1. 1.Training will include, at a minimum:
      1. a. Sanctuary City Code provisions and City policies;
      2. b. The distinction between administrative warrants and judicial warrants;
      3. c. The difference between and importance of public and nonpublic spaces, including authorized access to City spaces and facilities;
      4. d. Guidance on responding to inquiries or actions by a federal immigration authority, including requests for information regarding City employees or residents and visitors and attempts to access City property or City-sponsored meetings;
      5. e. The process for rapidly contacting the appropriate City official in urgent situations; and
      6. f. Training specific to supervisory responsibilities.
    2. 2. The training may also include, but is not limited to:
      1. a. Information on how and where employees can access relevant City resources and additional learning materials;
      2. b. Resources for City employees directly affected by federal immigration authority enforcement action; and
      3. c. Protocols for supervisors on responding if employees are detained, as well as guidance on compassionate leadership and support for employees.
    3. 3. The training will be reviewed no less than annually and may be reviewed more frequently as necessary. Revisions will incorporate emerging best practices, newly enacted laws, updated protocols, and relevant resources. Updates will be informed by feedback from Employee Resource Group representatives, relevant and representative bureaus, equity and language subject matter experts, labor union representatives, immigration rights organizations, faith leaders, community leaders, nonprofits, educational institutions and additional community partners.
  3. C. City-owned and leased spaces and buildings will display visible signage identifying entry requirements for the public and visitors and the specific areas which are public spaces and all areas that are not.
    1. 1. Signage will be in accordance with best practices for language access and plain language, and recommendations of Employee Resource Groups, equity and subject matter experts on immigrant affairs and rights.
    2. 2. Signage will include companion resources to explain the signage and contain additional resources and contacts. Companion resources will be based on best practices for language access and plain language, Sanctuary City trainings, and content should be in accordance with immigrant rights organization recommendations.
    3. 3. Signage policies and resources will be updated regularly and informed by experts, City Attorney advice, Employee Resource Groups and community leaders in language access, equity, immigrant affairs and rights, and additional relevant subject matters.
  4. D. Immigrant affairs tracking evaluation and reporting.
  5. The City will regularly review their existing programs and services to identify ways to comply with this Code Section, and implement best practices and policies for staff and communities impacted by immigration.
    1. 1. Every City bureau and office will provide the following information to Council at least quarterly:
      1. a.   Employee training completion rates;
      2. b.   Federal enforcement activity on City property and facilities; and
      3. c.   Known violations of the Sanctuary Promise Act by City employees.
    2. 2. The City will also provide an annual report to Council summarizing Freedom of Information Act requests, immigration enforcement communication, requests, and activities and a detailed description of the City's response.
    3. 3. The City will provide a report at least annually to Council. The report will be combined and coordinated. It will include the following:
      1. a.  An evaluation of training on City's sanctuary policies; and
      2. b.  Compliance with City's sanctuary policies; and
      3. c.   Information on sanctuary-related policies and procedures in similar local jurisdictions.
      4. d.  Reviewal and evaluation will be informed by feedback from Employee Resource Group representatives, relevant and representative bureaus, equity and language subject matter experts, labor union representatives, immigration rights organizations, faith leaders, community leaders, non-profits, educational institutions and additional community partners.

records.html:
Law enforcement oﬃcers who are easily identiﬁable promote transparency in their duties and strengthen trust between agencies and the communities they serve. An oﬃcer's visible face facilitates communication, allows for the reading of expressions, and helps reduce the risk of conﬂict in emotionally charged situations. Oﬃcers shall maintain professionalism by clearly identifying themselves when engaged in oﬃcial activity, ensuring that their appearance and conduct promote public conﬁdence and safety.Any person arrested in the City of Portland has the right to know the identity of the arresting officer.

This Chapter establishes standards for law enforcement oﬃcer identiﬁcation, veriﬁcation of apparent law enforcement activity occurring within the City, and the documentation of people presenting as oﬃcers. The City will comply with this Chapter in a manner consistent with all applicable federal and state laws.

1. A.  Oﬃcer means any sworn law enforcement oﬃcer employed by or operating under the jurisdiction of any government agency, or any person purporting to act under the color of law as a law enforcement officer.
  2. B.  PPB oﬃcer means any sworn employee of the Portland Police Bureau (PPB) acting within the scope of their oﬃcial duties.
  3. C.  Proof of identity means a government-issued identification that includes name and photograph of the carrier and a face free of any covering that inhibits the ability to verify that the person in possession of the identification is the person identified.
  4. D.  Preliminary investigation means the gathering or verification of information through lawful means. A preliminary investigation may be conducted through consensual contact and does not constitute a detention or seizure unless supported by reasonable suspicion or other lawful authority.
  5. E. Proof of authority means a person is acting within the scope of lawful authority of their law enforcement agency and shall be established by at least one indicia of authority. The indicia set forth below are illustrative and not exhaustive, and nothing herein precludes consideration of other objective evidence establishing lawful authority:
    1. 1.  A uniform clearly and visibly displaying a badge number, name, and agency identification;
    2. 2.  A judicial warrant establishing their authority;
    3. 3.  Official credentials or identification establishing an individual's confirmed law enforcement status;
    4. 4.  An appropriately marked vehicle for the entity that employs the law enforcement officer that is visible to individuals beyond such officer;
    5. 5.  The presence of other identifiable officers in uniform (defined as 23.30.020 E.1.); or
    6. 6. Authority verified through a law enforcement agency or dispatch center.
  6. F. Facial covering means any opaque mask, garment, helmet, headgear, balaclava, tactical mask, gaiter, ski mask or other item that conceals or obscures the facial identity of an individual. Facial covering does not include:
    1. 1. A medical-grade mask or respirator, including an N95 medical mask, worn to protect against the transmission of disease or infection;
    2. 2. Any mask, helmet, or device, including air purifying respirators, full or half masks or self-contained breathing apparatuses, necessary to protect against exposure to toxins, gas, smoke, flame or extreme or severely inclement weather;

    3. 3. A motorcycle or bicycle helmet worn while a law enforcement officer is operating a motorcycle, bicycle or other vehicle that requires a helmet for safe operation while in the performance of the officer's duties;

      4. A fire helmet worn during an arson investigation;

      5. Eyewear necessary to protect the eyes from physical objects or retinal weapons;

      6. A translucent face shield or clear mask that does not conceal the wearer's facial identity and is used in compliance with the employing law enforcement agency's policy.

  7. G.  Law enforcement activities means activities involving patrol, investigation, arrest, detention, or other direct enforcement of criminal laws, or of civil laws when enforcement involves detention. Law enforcement activities do not include appearances for testimony, training, or community engagement.
  8. H. Credible indicia of authority means proof of identity plus proof of authority. Proof of identity and authority may be established simultaneously when the government-issued identification possessed by the individual claiming law enforcement authority includes a name and photograph as well as law enforcement agency affiliation, and matches a face free of any covering. Credible indicia of authority may be established voluntarily, may be requested, or may be established by observation.

1. A. Officers may wear facial coverings when:
    1. 1. Engaged in undercover duties in the regular performance of the officer's official duties;
    2. 2. Assigned to a tactical response team, while actively performing tactical duties, if a facial covering is necessary to protect the officer's face from physical harm while performing such duties; or 
    3. 3. Working in extreme or severely inclement weather, including freezing temperatures, high wind or highly dusty conditions.
  2. B. For purposes of this Section, tactical response team includes:
    1. 1. A Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT) team;
    2. 2. A hazardous device, bomb or explosive ordnance disposal unit;
    3. 3. A chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or explosive (CBRNE) response unit; or
    4. 4. A tactical K-9 unit assigned to support high-risk warrant service, hostage rescue, armed barricade response or active shooter response.

1. A.  Compliance with State Law. All requirements of this Section shall be interpreted and applied in a manner consistent with Oregon law governing law enforcement identifiability requirements and the legal protections described in Section 23.30.080 of this Chapter. Officers operating within the City shall comply with this Chapter while on duty and actively engaged in official law enforcement activities.
  2. B.  Receipt of identiﬁcation.
    1. 1.  PPB officers shall receive oﬃcial Portland Police Bureau-issued identiﬁcation (badges, nametags, identiﬁcation cards, business cards, etc.) to be used for oﬃcial business.
    2. 2.  PPB officers shall ensure they have oﬃcial Portland Police Bureau-issued identiﬁcation and an adequate supply of PPB-issued business cards at all times while on duty.
  3. C.  Display of identiﬁcation.
    1. 1.  Oﬃcers shall visibly display their agency-issued badge, and permanent identifying number or nametag (including their last name) on their outermost garment and carry their agency-issued identiﬁcation document, except as outlined in Subsections 23.30.025 A.1. and 23.30.030 E.1.
    2. 2.  Oﬃcers operating in the City of Portland shall not intentionally conceal or obscure their faces through the use of facial coverings except as permitted under Oregon law and Section 23.30.025.
  4. D.  Providing identiﬁcation to the public.
    1. 1.  When practical, safe, and tactically feasible, PPB oﬃcers shall, upon request, identify themselves by name and oﬀer their PPB-issued business card containing their Department of Public Safety Standards and Training (DPSST) number.
    2. 2.  Any person arrested in the City of Portland has the right to know the identity of the arresting officer. When practical, safe, and tactically feasible, officers will identify themselves to the subject of arrest, holding, or detention.
  5. E.  Masking and identification exceptions.
    1. 1. Plainclothes operations. The requirements of Subsections 23.30.030 B., C., and D.1. do not apply to a law enforcement officer who:
      1. a.  Is engaged in undercover duties as part of the regular performance of the officer's official duties.
      2. b.  Is engaged in security or escort details as part of the regular performance of the officer's official duties.
      3. c.  Responds to exigent circumstances, if the officer is responding to those circumstances while off duty.
      4. d.  Is a detective assigned to and actively engaged in investigative duties, including interviewing victims and witnesses.
    2. 2.  Approval and documentation. When a facial-covering exemption under Subsections 23.30.025 A.2. and 3. is used by a PPB officer, the operational necessity must be documented. Exemptions taken under Subsection 23.30.025 A.2. must follow documentation requirements a-d below. Exemptions taken under Subsection 23.30.025 A.3. must follow documentation requirements Subsections b.-c. below:
      1. a.  The PPB oﬃcer's full name;
      2. b.  Assigned duties or deployment at the time of the exception;
      3. c.  The speciﬁc rationale for the exception; and
      4. d.  The name and rank of the supervising PPB officer who authorized the exception or who was notified and ratified the exception when prior approval was not practicable.
    3. 3.  Facial covering exceptions used by a law enforcement officer shall not be used to impair review of, or accountability for, their official actions.

1. A.  Scope. This Section applies when a person lacking immediate proof of authority is engaged in conduct that would be unlawful for a civilian but would be lawful only if the person were a sworn law enforcement officer acting within the scope of official duties.

    PPB officers shall make reasonable efforts to determine whether the person is, in fact, a law enforcement officer acting under lawful authority.  If such determination cannot immediately be made, an officer will proceed with a preliminary investigation.

    Verification procedures under this Chapter shall be implemented in a manner consistent with Oregon law.

  2. B.  Preliminary investigation. PPB officers will conduct a preliminary investigation.PPB officers will notify a supervisor and investigate the situation for a potential criminal act. Officers will contact possible agencies or dispatch centers to verify their authority.
  3. Preliminary investigations may continue until PPB, based upon the totality of the circumstances, determines whether reasonable suspicion exists to believe the person has committed, is committing, or is about to commit a criminal offense.
  4. C.  Investigations with reasonable suspicion. When reasonable suspicion exists based on the totality of circumstances including but not limited to information gathered in the preliminary investigation in Subsection 23.30.050 B., that the person has committed, is committing, or is about to commit a criminal offense, PPB officers will treat the situation as a potential criminal act, as permitted by law and may detain the person.
    1. 1.  Any commands, restraint, or detention must be limited in scope and duration to what is reasonably necessary to confirm or dispel the officer's reasonable suspicion and to address legitimate safety concerns.
    2. 2.  PPB officers will, when supported by reasonable suspicion and as permitted by law, issue commands, restrain, or detain the person claiming to be a law enforcement officer to preserve public safety, and investigate the conduct.
    3. 3.  If it is determined that the person is a law enforcement officer acting within the scope of lawful duties, PPB officers shall promptly end any continued detention or restraint and document the circumstances of the encounter.

1. A.  Scope. This Section refers to all police actions and encounters undertaken as outlined in Section 23.30.050.
    1. 1.  Incident reporting and documentation. All police actions and encounters will be documented in writing including the time and location of the incident; what instigated police involvement; indicia of authority observed or absent; steps taken to verify law enforcement authority; and the outcome.
    2. The written report will also include whether the conduct is determined to be criminal, and any relevant police report number. The written report will include, if known, the investigated law enforcement officer's name, badge number, and agency. If the PPB officer observed that the person in question was wearing a mask, or was not wearing a badge, or was not wearing either a permanent identifying number or a name tag, the report shall include that information.
    3. 2. Body-worn camera. Where possible, encounters should be recorded on body-worn camera to the extent allowed by law and in accordance with Portland Police Bureau body-worn camera policy. Body-worn camera footage under this Section will be retained by the City for the maximum period allowed by law.

A violation of this Chapter does not constitute a criminal offense and is not subject to the general penalty provisions of Portland City Code Section 1.01.110.

This Chapter regulates the conduct of law enforcement officers and agencies while performing official duties and shall be implemented through administrative, supervisory, employment, or civil processes authorized by law.

The Mayor or Council by resolution may authorize the City of Portland to bring a lawsuit seeking injunctive relief requiring officers of an agency to abide by the masking and identification standards of this Chapter that apply to such officers.
